title: Boxing and the Newspaper
bigQuestion: How did newspapers and radio turn prizefighting into a public story, even while many states and school leagues kept boxing out?

story.title: A Fight on the Front Page
story.kicker: A city paper sells a fight that no school would ever host.
paragraphs: It is September 1927 in Chicago. A newsboy on State Street shouts the headline. Jack Dempsey will fight Gene Tunney at Soldier Field, the new stadium on the lakefront. Tunney took the heavyweight title from Dempsey a year earlier in Philadelphia. Now the city will host the rematch.

The newspaper fills whole pages. It prints each boxer's weight and reach. It prints where they trained and what they ate. It sells the fight as a story with a hero, a challenger and a question: can the old champion win back his crown?

On the night of September 22, more than 100,000 people fill the stadium. Millions more listen on radio across the country. In the seventh round Tunney goes down. The referee waits for Dempsey to move to a neutral corner before counting. Tunney rises and wins. People still argue about the long count.

That same fall, Illinois high schools run football, basketball and track under the IHSA. None of them has a boxing team. The fight belongs to promoters, papers and paying crowds, not to the school board. This chapter asks how both of those facts could be true in one city.
story.think: Why might a newspaper want a big fight in its city, even if schools want nothing to do with boxing?

lessons.title: Bare Knuckles and the London Rules
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s prizefighting was fought with bare fists under the London Prize Ring Rules and was illegal in most places.
reading: A *prizefight* is a fight for money, often a purse put up by backers and a crowd. In Britain in the early 1800s, these fights were fought with bare fists. Crowds gathered in fields outside towns. They often moved at the last minute to escape the police.

Fighters needed a shared paper to settle disputes. The *London Prize Ring Rules* were written in 1838 and revised in 1853. They set a square ring with ropes. A round ended only when a man went down. So a fight could last for dozens of rounds and for hours.

In the United States, most states made prizefighting a crime in the 1800s. Lawmakers worried about injuries, gambling and rowdy crowds. So fights happened on barges, on islands and across state lines. The sport grew in secret places while newspapers told the story in public.

words.d: a boxing match fought for a money prize, often called a purse
the bare-knuckle boxing rules written in 1838 and revised in 1853

look.title: Where Is the Ring Tonight?
look.text: A notice passes from hand to hand in 1880. It gives no address. It says only: take the morning train south and follow the crowd off at the river. The fighters, the stakes and the time are listed. The place is kept secret until the last hour.
look.prompt: Why would a fight notice in 1880 hide the place until the last hour?

check.q: What is a prizefight?
choices: A fight for a money prize
check.why: A prizefight is a boxing match fought for a purse of money.

check.q: When were the London Prize Ring Rules first written?
check.why: The London Prize Ring Rules were written in 1838 and revised in 1853.

check.q: Why did many fights in the 1800s happen on barges or islands?
choices: Prizefighting was illegal in most states
Schools owned the land in towns
check.why: Most states banned prizefighting, so promoters looked for places out of reach of the police.

lessons.title: Sullivan, Kilrain and the Last Bare-Knuckle Title
lessons.mainIdea: The 1889 Sullivan–Kilrain fight in Mississippi was the last heavyweight title fight with bare knuckles.
reading: John L. Sullivan was born in Boston in 1858. He became the most famous athlete in America in the 1880s. He toured the country and offered money to anyone who could last a set time with him. Crowds and newspapers followed him from town to town.

On July 8, 1889, Sullivan fought Jake Kilrain near Richburg, Mississippi. The fight was illegal, so the place was kept secret. Special trains carried fans from New Orleans. The two men fought 75 rounds in the summer heat before Kilrain's side gave up.

This was the last heavyweight *championship* fought with bare knuckles. Sullivan was later arrested and fined for the fight. Newspapers across the country had sent reporters. Their long reports made the fight a national event, even though it broke the law.

words.d: the title that goes to the winner judged best in a sport or weight class
the heaviest weight class in boxing

look.title: How Many Rounds?
look.cite: Heavyweight title fight records as reported in newspapers of each year
look.prompt: Which fight lasted longest? What rule change helps explain why the later fights were shorter?

check.q: Where was the Sullivan–Kilrain fight held in 1889?
choices: Madison Square Garden in New York
check.why: The 1889 fight was held in secret near Richburg, Mississippi.

check.q: Why does the 1889 fight matter in boxing history?
choices: It was the last heavyweight title fight with bare knuckles
It was the first fight on radio
It was the first Olympic boxing match
It was the first fight held in a school
check.why: Sullivan–Kilrain was the last heavyweight championship fought with bare fists.

check.q: How did most Americans learn about the fight?
check.why: Reporters sent long stories to papers across the country; radio came decades later.

lessons.title: Gloves and the 1892 Title Fight
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892 the heavyweight title changed hands in a gloved fight under the Queensberry rules in New Orleans.
reading: The *Queensberry rules*, published in 1867, required padded gloves and three-minute rounds. A fighter who went down had ten seconds to rise. These rules made fights shorter and gave referees a clearer count. Promoters liked them, because a gloved fight looked less like a street brawl.

On September 7, 1892, Sullivan fought James J. Corbett at the Olympic Club in New Orleans. They wore gloves and fought under the Queensberry rules. Corbett, a former bank clerk from San Francisco, won in the 21st round. Sullivan lost his title for the first time.

New Orleans allowed the fight because it was held by a club under the new rules. Gloves helped boxing argue that it was a sport, not a riot. Still, most states kept their bans. The gloved title fight became the model that later laws would regulate.

words.d: boxing rules published in 1867 that required gloves and three-minute rounds
a person who organizes and sells a fight or event for profit

look.title: Two Rule Books Side by Side
look.text: London Prize Ring Rules (1838): bare fists; a round ends when a man goes down; no set length for a round. Queensberry rules (1867): padded gloves; three-minute rounds with a rest; a fighter who goes down has ten seconds to rise.
look.prompt: Which rule book would a city leader find easier to allow? Give two reasons from the rules.

check.q: Who won the heavyweight title in New Orleans in 1892?
check.why: Corbett beat Sullivan in the 21st round on September 7, 1892.

check.q: What did the Queensberry rules require?
choices: Bare fists and no time limit
check.why: The 1867 Queensberry rules required gloves and three-minute rounds.

check.q: Why did gloves help boxing's public image?
choices: A gloved fight looked more like a sport than a brawl
Gloves were required by the Olympics in 1892
check.why: Promoters used gloves and set rounds to argue boxing was a regulated sport.

lessons.title: The Sports Page and the Police Gazette
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s newspapers and the Police Gazette used boxing to sell papers and even gave out championship belts.
reading: In the 1880s big city newspapers began to build sports departments. Editors saw that sports news sold papers every day. Boxing was perfect for them. A fight had two names, a date and a winner, and it could be argued about for weeks.

The *National Police Gazette* was a New York weekly paper. Richard K. Fox took it over in 1877. He filled it with crime stories, pictures and boxing. Fox offered prize money and awarded championship belts. His paper did not just report fights; it helped create them.

This made the press part of the sport. Papers named champions, printed challenges between fighters and hired writers who knew the fighters. A reader in a small town could follow a fight he would never see. The *sports page* became a public room for a sport that was often banned.

words.d: a New York weekly paper that covered crime and boxing and gave out title belts
the part of a newspaper that reports games, fights and scores

look.title: A Challenge in Print
look.text: Picture a page from an 1880s sporting paper. A boxing column prints a letter from one fighter's backer. It offers a set sum of money to any man who will meet him. The editor adds that the paper will hold the stakes and name the winner champion.
look.prompt: What jobs is the newspaper doing here besides reporting the news?

check.q: Who took over the National Police Gazette in 1877?
check.why: Richard K. Fox ran the Police Gazette and used it to promote boxing.

check.q: Why did editors like boxing news?
choices: It sold papers and could be argued about for weeks
check.why: Boxing had clear names, dates and winners that kept readers buying papers.

check.q: How did the Police Gazette go beyond reporting?
choices: It built boxing rings in schools
It awarded belts and prize money
check.why: Fox's paper offered prizes and belts, helping to create fights and champions.

lessons.title: Jack Johnson and the Color Line
lessons.mainIdea: Jack Johnson became the first Black heavyweight champion in 1908, and his victories set off a public backlash.
reading: Jack Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878. For years white champions refused to fight Black challengers for the heavyweight title. This refusal was boxing's own *color line*. Johnson followed champion Tommy Burns around the world, demanding a chance.

On December 26, 1908, Johnson beat Burns in Sydney, Australia. He became the first Black heavyweight champion. Many white newspapers called for a "great white hope" to take the title back. Former champion Jim Jeffries came out of retirement to try.

On July 4, 1910, Johnson beat Jeffries in Reno, Nevada, in the 15th round. After the news spread, white mobs attacked Black people in cities across the country, and people were killed. Johnson later lived in Chicago. In 1912 he opened a nightclub there called the Café de Champion.

words.d: a barrier, written or unwritten, that kept Black people out of a sport or place
a fighter who tries to take the title from the champion

look.title: Two Headlines, One Night
look.text: It is July 5, 1910. One paper's headline says the champion has proved himself beyond doubt. Another paper, in a different city, reports that crowds attacked Black residents on the streets after the news arrived by telegraph.
look.prompt: What does the pair of headlines show about how one fight could mean different things to different readers?

check.q: When did Jack Johnson win the heavyweight title?
check.why: Johnson beat Tommy Burns in Sydney on December 26, 1908.

check.q: What happened after Johnson beat Jeffries in 1910?
choices: White mobs attacked Black people in many cities
check.why: The Reno result was followed by violence against Black Americans across the country.

check.q: What did Johnson open in Chicago in 1912?
check.why: Johnson opened the Café de Champion nightclub in Chicago in 1912.

lessons.title: A Law Against Fight Films
lessons.mainIdea: In 1912 Congress banned carrying prizefight films across state lines, a law that stood until 1940.
reading: By 1910 fights were filmed and shown in theaters. The film of Johnson beating Jeffries worried many white officials. Cities and states moved to stop it from being shown. Leaders feared that the pictures of a Black champion would cause more unrest.

In 1912 Congress passed the *Sims Act*. It made it a federal crime to carry films of prizefights across state lines for showing. The law hit the fight film business hard. A film could still be shown in the state where the fight took place.

The Sims Act stayed in force until 1940. It shows that the government treated boxing pictures as a public danger, not just entertainment. Historians link the law directly to Johnson's victories. It is an example of *censorship*, when officials stop people from seeing or reading something.

words.d: a 1912 federal law that banned moving prizefight films across state lines
when officials stop people from seeing, hearing or reading something

look.title: The Fight Film Law
look.text: Congress made it unlawful to bring into the United States, or to carry from one state to another, any film or picture of a prizefight meant to be shown to the public.
look.cite: Sims Act, Act of July 31, 1912, United States Statutes at Large
look.prompt: The law never names Jack Johnson. What evidence would a historian use to connect the law to him?

check.q: What did the Sims Act ban?
choices: All boxing in the United States
Carrying prizefight films across state lines
check.why: The 1912 Sims Act banned interstate transport of prizefight films.

check.q: How long did the Sims Act stay in force?
check.why: The law was passed in 1912 and ended in 1940.

check.q: What is censorship?
choices: A count of the people at a fight
Officials stopping people from seeing or reading something
check.why: Censorship means officials block what the public may see, hear or read.

lessons.title: New York's Athletic Commission
lessons.mainIdea: The Walker Law of 1920 made boxing legal in New York under a state athletic commission that licensed fighters and set rules.
reading: New York changed its mind about boxing several times. It allowed fights for a few years, then banned them again. In 1920 the state passed the *Walker Law*, named for state senator Jimmy Walker. It made boxing legal again, this time with a state office to watch over it.

That office was the New York State Athletic Commission, an *athletic commission*. It licensed boxers, referees, judges and promoters. It required doctors at fights. It could suspend a fighter or hold back a purse. The ban-and-allow cycle gave way to regulation, which means rules enforced by an official body.

Other states copied the idea. By the late 1920s many states had boxing commissions. Boxing had moved from barges and secret trains into licensed arenas. In 1925 promoter Tex Rickard opened a new Madison Square Garden in New York, built largely for boxing.

words.d: the 1920 New York law that made boxing legal under a state commission
a state body that licenses fighters and officials and sets boxing rules
rules made and enforced by an official body

look.title: Steps Toward a Regulated Sport
look.cite: Boxing rule histories; United States Statutes at Large; New York State session laws
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first bare-knuckle rule book and the Walker Law?

check.q: What did the Walker Law of 1920 do?
choices: Made boxing legal in New York under a state commission
check.why: The Walker Law legalized boxing in New York and set up a state athletic commission.

check.q: What does an athletic commission do?
choices: Licenses fighters and officials and sets rules
check.why: A commission is a state body that licenses and regulates boxing.

check.q: Who opened a new Madison Square Garden in 1925?
check.why: Promoter Tex Rickard opened the new Garden in 1925.

lessons.title: Boxing Goes on the Air
lessons.mainIdea: Radio carried the 1921 Dempsey–Carpentier fight to a huge audience and made heavyweight fights national events heard live.
reading: Commercial radio began in the United States in 1920. KDKA in Pittsburgh went on the air that November. Within months, stations looked for live events that listeners would want. A fight was ideal, because it happened at one time and had a clear result.

On July 2, 1921, Jack Dempsey fought Georges Carpentier of France in Jersey City, New Jersey. Tex Rickard built a wooden arena for the crowd. The fight earned more than one million dollars in tickets. A radio hookup sent a round-by-round account to listeners at gatherings in many towns.

Radio changed what it meant to follow a fight. A newspaper told you what happened yesterday. A *broadcast* told you what was happening now. Fighters became voices and names in millions of living rooms. The *gate*, or ticket money, also grew as fame spread.

words.d: a radio or television program sent out to many listeners at once
the money a sports event takes in from ticket sales

look.title: Newspaper Versus Radio
look.text: A farmer in 1921 reads about a big fight in the next morning's paper. His neighbor sits by a radio in the town hall the night before and hears each round called as it happens.
look.prompt: What does the radio listener get that the newspaper reader does not? What might the reader get that the listener misses?

check.q: Who fought Jack Dempsey on July 2, 1921?
check.why: Dempsey fought Georges Carpentier of France in Jersey City in 1921.

check.q: What is the gate of a fight?
choices: The money taken in from ticket sales
check.why: The gate is the ticket money an event earns.

check.q: How was radio different from a newspaper for fans?
choices: Radio was banned by the Sims Act
Radio told what was happening live
check.why: A broadcast carried events as they happened; papers reported them later.

lessons.title: The Long Count at Soldier Field
lessons.mainIdea: The 1927 Dempsey–Tunney rematch in Chicago drew more than 100,000 people and set off a long public argument over one count.
reading: Gene Tunney took the heavyweight title from Jack Dempsey in Philadelphia in September 1926. The rematch was set for Chicago's Soldier Field on September 22, 1927. More than 100,000 people came. The ticket money was more than two million dollars, a record for the time.

In the seventh round Dempsey knocked Tunney down. A newer rule said the standing fighter must go to a *neutral corner* before the count began. Dempsey did not go at once. The referee's count started late, and Tunney rose before ten. Tunney won the fight on points.

Newspapers and radio audiences argued for years about the "long count." It showed how a written rule, applied by one official, could decide a championship. It also showed that Chicago could host an event as large as any in the country.

words.d: a ring corner that belongs to neither fighter's team
a second fight between the same two opponents

look.title: A Rule and a Referee
look.text: The rule is printed plainly: when one boxer is down, the other must go to the farthest neutral corner, and the count starts only after he gets there. On the night, one man stands over the other for several seconds.
look.prompt: Was the referee right to wait? Use the rule to explain your answer.

check.q: Where was the 1927 Dempsey–Tunney rematch held?
check.why: The rematch took place at Soldier Field on September 22, 1927.

check.q: Why is it called the long count?
choices: The count started late because Dempsey did not go to a neutral corner
The crowd count took a week
check.why: The referee waited for Dempsey to reach a neutral corner, so Tunney had extra seconds.

check.q: About how many people attended the 1927 rematch?
check.why: More than 100,000 people filled Soldier Field.

lessons.title: Golden Gloves and Chicago Youth Boxing
lessons.mainIdea: In Chicago, newspapers and the Catholic Youth Organization ran amateur boxing for young people outside the school leagues.
reading: In the 1920s the Chicago Tribune ran an *amateur* boxing tournament called the Golden Gloves. Tribune sports editor Arch Ward promoted it. The New York Daily News ran its own Golden Gloves. Later the two cities sent teams to fight each other, and the papers filled pages with the results.

In 1930 Bishop Bernard Sheil founded the Catholic Youth Organization, or CYO, in Chicago. Boxing was one of its biggest programs. Its tournaments drew large crowds. The CYO accepted boys of different faiths and races, which was not true of every club in the city.

These programs met in parish halls, park field houses and club gyms. They were town rooms, not school rooms. A teenager could train at night and fight in a newspaper tournament. The same teenager might play basketball for his high school under the IHSA by day.

words.d: an athlete who competes without being paid
amateur boxing tournaments first run by newspapers in Chicago and New York
a youth program founded in Chicago in 1930 by Bishop Bernard Sheil

look.title: Chicago Boxing Rooms and Nights
rows: Louis wins title at Comiskey Park
look.cite: Chicago Tribune reports; Chicago Park District and CYO histories
look.prompt: Which of these rooms was built for crowds, and which was built for young people?

check.q: Who founded the Catholic Youth Organization in Chicago in 1930?
check.why: Bishop Bernard Sheil founded the CYO in 1930.

check.q: What does amateur mean?
check.why: An amateur competes without pay.

check.q: Which newspaper ran Chicago's Golden Gloves?
check.why: The Chicago Tribune, with sports editor Arch Ward, ran the Chicago tournament.

lessons.title: Joe Louis and Two Famous Nights
lessons.mainIdea: Joe Louis won the heavyweight title in Chicago in 1937, and his 1938 win over Max Schmeling was heard on radio around the world.
reading: Joe Louis grew up in Detroit and learned to box at a city recreation center. On June 22, 1937, he beat James Braddock at Comiskey Park in Chicago. He became the second Black heavyweight champion, 22 years after Jack Johnson lost the title.

Max Schmeling of Germany had beaten Louis in 1936. By 1938 Germany was ruled by the Nazi Party, which claimed that one race was superior. The rematch at Yankee Stadium on June 22, 1938, became a symbol of a fight between nations and ideas. Louis won in the first round.

Tens of millions of people heard the fight on radio. Many white newspapers that once mocked Black fighters now called Louis an American hero. Louis held the title until 1949. His career showed how the press and radio could turn a boxer into a *symbol* for a whole country.

words.d: a person or thing that stands for a bigger idea
the party that ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945 and preached racist ideas

look.title: A Two-Minute Fight on the Radio
look.text: On a June night in 1938, families gather around radios in Harlem, on Chicago's South Side and in towns across the country. The announcer's call lasts barely two minutes. Crowds pour into the streets to celebrate.
look.prompt: Why might so many people have cared so much about a fight that lasted barely two minutes?

check.q: Where did Joe Louis win the heavyweight title in 1937?
check.why: Louis beat James Braddock at Comiskey Park on June 22, 1937.

check.q: Why was the 1938 Louis–Schmeling fight seen as more than a sports event?
choices: It was the first gloved fight
It was the first fight in a school
It was treated as a contest between the United States and Nazi Germany
check.why: The rematch came as Nazi Germany preached racial superiority, so many saw it as a clash of nations and ideas.

check.q: How long did the 1938 rematch last?
check.why: Louis won in the first round.

lessons.title: Why School Leagues Kept Boxing Out
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois school sport under the IHSA never took boxing in, and the NCAA dropped college boxing after a death in 1960.
reading: The IHSA was founded in 1900 to run high school contests in Illinois. It added sports such as basketball, track, tennis and swimming. It never ran a boxing state series. For Illinois teenagers, boxing lived in parks, parish halls and newspaper tournaments.

Colleges did try boxing. The NCAA held national boxing championships starting in 1932. In the 1960 tournament, Charlie Mohr of the University of Wisconsin was hurt in a bout and died days later. The NCAA ended boxing as a championship sport after that season.

School leaders gave reasons that echoed the 1800s: the risk of head injury and the link between boxing and money. Schools kept sports they could defend to parents and boards. Boxing remained a town gym and professional sport. It also stayed an Olympic sport, as it had been since 1904.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900, which runs state high school contests
the National Collegiate Athletic Association, which runs college sport championships

look.title: Town Gym or School League?
look.text: A school board meeting in the 1930s. One member says a boxing team would give tough boys a place to belong. Another says the school cannot risk injuries and does not want ties to fight money. A parent notes that the CYO already holds boxing nights at the parish hall.
look.prompt: Which side would the IHSA's choice support? What does the parent's point add?

check.q: What happened to NCAA boxing after 1960?
choices: The NCAA ended it as a championship sport
check.why: After Charlie Mohr died following the 1960 tournament, the NCAA dropped boxing.

check.q: Where did Illinois teenagers box, since the IHSA had no boxing series?
choices: In high school gyms under IHSA rules
Parks, parish halls and newspaper tournaments
check.why: Boxing lived in town rooms like park field houses, CYO halls and the Golden Gloves.

check.q: Since when has boxing been an Olympic sport?
check.why: Boxing has been on the Olympic program since the 1904 Games in St. Louis.

review.q: Which rule book required padded gloves and three-minute rounds?
review.why: The Queensberry rules of 1867 required gloves and timed rounds.

review.q: Why were many 1800s prizefights held in secret places?
choices: Prizefighting was illegal in most states
review.why: Most states banned prizefights, so promoters hid them from police.

review.q: What role did the National Police Gazette play?
choices: It licensed fighters for New York
It promoted fights and gave out belts
review.why: Richard K. Fox's paper reported, promoted and awarded prizes in boxing.

review.q: What was the Sims Act of 1912 a response to?
review.why: Congress passed the fight film ban after Johnson's 1910 win over Jeffries.

review.q: How did the Walker Law change boxing in New York?
choices: It legalized boxing under a licensing commission
It gave boxing to the schools
review.why: The 1920 Walker Law created a state athletic commission to regulate boxing.

review.q: Which event is linked to Soldier Field in 1927?
review.why: The Dempsey–Tunney rematch with the long count was held at Soldier Field.

review.q: What did radio add to following a fight?
choices: Reading a box score the next day
Hearing it live as it happened
review.why: Radio broadcasts carried fights live to listeners far away.

review.q: How did boxing's place in Illinois differ from basketball's?
choices: Boxing had an IHSA series; basketball did not
Both were run only by newspapers

review.why: The IHSA ran basketball but never boxing, which stayed in parks, parishes and paper tournaments.
